stories.title: District official charged with homicide over ferry disaster that killed 97 people
stories.summary: Police in Zimbabwe have arrested a district official charged with culpable homicide over the sinking of a government-run ferry that claimed at least 97 lives. The 49-year-old district coordinator for the state-run Rural Infrastructure Development Agency has appeared in court and remains in custody, police said on Wednesday. The overloaded vessel capsized in bad weather on August 11 on Lake Kariba on the border with Zambia. Estimates put the number of passengers at more than 150 on a ferry authorised to carry just 90 people. At least 30 children under the age of 10 were among the dead. Seventy-seven people were rescued. Lake Kariba straddles the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia. It’s the world's largest man-made lake by volume. The ferry serves as a crucial transport link between Kariba town and remote communities.

stories.title: How to watch the partial lunar eclipse from Northern Ireland
stories.summary: Stargazers have the chance to see a stunning partial lunar eclipse early on Friday morning, as the moon enters Earth's shadow. At its peak, roughly 93% of the Moon's diameter will be covered, making the event look close to a total eclipse. For people in Northern Ireland hoping to catch a glimpse, the biggest challenge will be the early start, possible cloud cover, and the Moon's low position in the western sky. More than 90% of the Moon will be eclipsed shortly after 5am. What time is the lunar eclipse? The first phase of the eclipse begins at 02:23 BST when the Moon enters the lighter outer part of Earth's shadow, known as the penumbra. The much more obvious stage starts at 03:33, as Earth's darker central shadow begins moving across the lunar surface, with maximum eclipse occurring at 05:12, external. In Belfast, the Moon will be will be low in the western sky at about nine degrees with the eclipse ending at 06:34. In Dublin, it will be slightly higher in the sky and last until 06:38. Further west, viewers may have slightly longer before the moon disappears. In Enniskillen, moonset is 06:41, external. This means that visibility will not only depend on cloud cover, but also having an unobstructed view towards the west.

stories.title: Wild swimming linked to higher risk of stomach bugs and skin rashes
stories.summary: Findings from research into illnesses associated with bathing in lakes and rivers come amid boom in hobby Wild swimming has been linked to a higher risk of stomach bugs and skin rashes, according to the largest ever controlled study of illnesses associated with bathing in rivers and lakes. The research found that swimmers at locations in Hungary were more than twice as likely to develop skin problems, while the risk of contracting a stomach bug rose significantly in water with higher concentrations of E coli and other bacteria linked to faecal pollution. stories.title: Food waste processing is 'worth the extra effort'
stories.summary: Understanding the benefits of recycling food waste could encourage more people to do it in future, Cornwall Council has said. For the past two years, leftover food has been able to be taken to an anaerobic digester to be converted into methane to generate electricity and produce fertiliser. The council said about 36,000 tonnes of food waste had been recycled to date since the introduction of its new waste service. It said it hoped increased participation through understanding the benefits would help meet its target to recycle nearly two-thirds of Cornwall's waste by 2029. Cornwall's food waste is taken to a digester in Holsworthy, Devon, operated by Severn Trent Green Power. Chris Lofts, the site manager, said the waste was first filtered before having water added and being fed into a digester to create methane. "That methane we use as a fuel for engines that run generators and the generators produce electricity - and we then inject the electricity back into the National Grid," he explained. He said they tried to make sure nothing went to waste: "We use the heat as well to pasteurise the material on site for ancillary services that we do here. "Even the by-product, the digestate that comes out - that's used as a fertiliser for farmers to fertilise the countryside and make all the flowers and crops grow." Lofts said recycling food was better for the environment than just throwing it in the bin with other waste to be taken to an incinerator. He said: "The incinerators use the waste as a fuel - they burn it and heat up steam generators from that. But there is a residual, the ash, which needs to go somewhere.
